maintopic: GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF FIRST CANADIAN ARMY COMMANDER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF FIRST CANADIAN ARMY COMMANDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will be saddened to learn that an hour or two ago a member of the privy council passed away. He was also the commander of the only Canadian army we have had in the field; I refer to General H. D. G. Crerar.
As hon. members know, he was a man who served Canada for more than half a century in war and in peace with quiet efficiency, with sincerity and with great devotion. We shall miss him greatly-especially those of us privileged to be his friends-and we are grateful for what he has done for our country. I shall send my deep and heartfelt sympathy to Mrs. Crerar and to the family.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF FIRST CANADIAN ARMY COMMANDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great sorrow that we have learned of the sudden passing of our wartime commander. Those of us who
had the privilege of serving under General Crerar had the greatest admiration for his work and for the courage and inspiration that he transmitted to the forces under his command. He served with distinction as commander of Canada's first army in the field. On behalf of this party I should like to express our sympathy to his family.

maintopic: GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF FIRST CANADIAN ARMY COMMANDER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate the members of this party with the expressions of regret which have just been enunciated by the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. We too would like to express our great appreciation of the service which General Crerar has rendered this country both in war and in peace. At the invitation of General McNaughton it was my privilege during the war to visit the Canadian forces overseas, particularly Saskatchewan troops, and I shall always be grateful for the kindness and hospitality which were extended to me by General Crerar. I have very happy memories of that brief association with him and of the several occasions on which I have met him since. I think he was a great soldier and a fine Canadian, and we pay tribute to his memory.

maintopic: GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF FIRST CANADIAN ARMY COMMANDER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we too associate ourselves with the words of the Prime Minister on the passing of General Crerar. Truly Canada has lost one of her great citizens. All of us who have known him personally understand just how well he served this country. I am sure the people of the nation will join with us in our expression of sorrow and sympathy to the members of his family. Canada has lost a man who truly served her well. We have known of his illness and of the difficult days he has had in recent months. I am sure many of his friends have appreciated in a special way his services to Canada.

maintopic: GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF FIRST CANADIAN ARMY COMMANDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and others who have expressed their deep sympathy on the occasion of the death of General Crerar who was, we agree, a great Canadian.

To all his family, we extend our most sincere and deepest sympathy.

["Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question, and I welcome the

opportunity of making a comment on the appeal.
As hon. members are aware, representatives of some 14 non-aligned nations met in Belgrade two weeks ago at the instance of the government of Yugoslavia in an attempt to work out an appeal for a peaceful settlement of the problem in Viet Nam. I might add that a few days ago the Yugoslav ambassador called on the Prime Minister.
We have been following the deliberations of the Belgrade group with considerable interest as a manifestation of the genuine concern felt everywhere in the world at the development of the conflict in Viet Nam and its potential dangers for world peace. I believe that any constructive initiative aimed at reducing tensions in the first instance, and in a longer view at achieving an equitable long term solution, deserves commendation and encouragement.
I have not yet had an adequate opportunity to study the text of the Belgrade appeal in as much detail as I would like, but on the basis of a first reading I think there is much in it that we can support. In expressing grave concern over the aggravation of existing tensions, in reaffirming a belief in the inviolability of and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, and in advocating a peaceful solution through negotiations, the appeal seems firmly rooted in principles which are cornerstones of Canadian foreign policy.
Moreover, I believe the appeal has been formulated in such a way as to avoid dangerous oversimplifications of the complex factors contributing to the tension in Viet Nam. It would appear to me that ideas such as the unacceptability of the use of force and the dangers of outside intervention, including military intervention, are intended to have a general applicability to all those directly involved in this conflict. Only if there is widespread recognition of the fact that these ideas in particular, and the appeal in general, are directed with equal persuasive intent to all parties to this dispute can there be any prospect of this initiative bearing the fruits of success which we hope it may have."]

I might add that a few days ago the Yugoslav ambassador called on the Prime Minister.
We have been following the deliberations of the Belgrade group with considerable interest as a manifestation of the genuine concern felt everywhere in the world at the development of the conflict in Viet Nam and its potential dangers for world peace. I believe that any constructive initiative aimed at reducing tensions in the first instance, and in a longer view at achieving an equitable long term solution, deserves commendation and encouragement.
I have not yet had an adequate opportunity to study the text of the Belgrade appeal in as much detail as I would like, but on the basis of a first reading I think there is much in it that we can support. In expressing grave concern over the aggravation of existing tensions, in reaffirming a belief in the inviolability of and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, and in advocating a peaceful solution through negotiations, the appeal seems firmly rooted in principles which are cornerstones of Canadian foreign policy.
Moreover, I believe the appeal has been formulated in such a way as to avoid dangerous oversimplifications of the complex factors contributing to the tension in Viet Nam. It would appear to me that ideas such as the unacceptability of the use of force and the dangers of outside intervention, including military intervention, are intended to have a general applicability to all those directly involved in this conflict. subtopic: APPEAL OF SOVIET UNION FOR DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: APPEAL OF SOVIET UNION FOR DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question. May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs what response the government of Canada intends to make to the appeal of the Soviet union for a disarmament conference to be attended by all members of the United Nations?

subtopic: APPEAL OF SOVIET UNION FOR DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
speechtext: The Soviet union has called for a meeting of the 114 members of the United Nations. I think experience at the United Nations indicates that disarmament discussions are generally more efficient in a smaller group. It was for this reason that the United Nations endorsed the 18 nation disarmament committee which normally meets in Geneva. Canada is a member of that committee. We would prefer that there be a reconvening of the 18 power group. However, if there should be a meeting of the 114 nations to discuss disarmament Canada would, of course, participate fully.

subtopic: APPEAL OF SOVIET UNION FOR DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would the Secretary of State for External Affairs agree that the likelihood of success would be considerably limited if the government of mainland China were not represented at such a disarmament conference? speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPEAL OF SOVIET UNION FOR DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Of course disarmament cannot be fully achieved unless there is participation at some stage by all countries, particularly by the great powers, the countries which have a pre-eminent role in armaments. The hon. member's question involves a policy consideration which, of course, I cannot deal with except at the appropriate moment.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUGGESTED RESTRICTION IN POSSIBLE SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago I asked the Prime Minister a question with regard to the negotiations with France in con-

Inquiries of the Ministry nection with the sale of uranium by Canadian corporations, and the Prime Minister said he would give an answer to the house shortly.
I would ask him whether the Canadian government has insisted that inspectors be sent to France to find out for what purpose the uranium is to be used, and whether it is a fact that very recently, within the past few days or weeks at the outside, while these negotiations have been going on the United States has been able to sell some $75 million worth of uranium to France.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUGGESTED RESTRICTION IN POSSIBLE SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the last observation of my right hon. friend is concerned I have no information. His statement that the United States has sold uranium to France recently is a great surprise to me, and I would certainly want to look into that matter right away.
As far as the negotiations themselves are concerned, they are actively under consideration at the moment. There was a meeting held yesterday and there will be another meeting this afternoon, I believe, between those concerned.

subtopic: SUGGESTED RESTRICTION IN POSSIBLE SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister say whether Canada is insisting that the purposes for which this uranium will be purchased must be peaceful ones?

subtopic: SUGGESTED RESTRICTION IN POSSIBLE SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext: As I have already said, Mr. Speaker, we have international commitments in this regard which we propose to discharge in connection with any arrangements which might be reached.

subtopic: SUGGESTED RESTRICTION IN POSSIBLE SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister say whether one of the international arrangements is that the uranium which is sold must not be used for anything other than peaceful objectives and purposes?

subtopic: SUGGESTED RESTRICTION IN POSSIBLE SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext: That is right, Mr. Speaker. The commitments are that the uranium we sell be used for peaceful purposes.

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State.
In view of the long hours worked by the interpreters and translators of the House of Commons or the various government services, does the minister intend to give them a bonus or a raise or even pay them time and a half or double time after a certain number of hours of work, as is done in private industry?

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question of salaries and other problems related to the translation service are now under consideration so that this service can be made as efficient as possible.

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Does the minister intend to take similar action in the case of interpreters because they too are bilingual and are doing a tremendous job?

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, interpreters come under the translation service.

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question. I have here a notice of a Civil Service Commission of Canada competition received this morning, and it states:
Interesting career as translators from English into French, for university graduates and experienced persons.
According to this competition notice, salaries offered are $4,500 and $4,600 per year. Does the minister really think skilled translators can be obtained by offering such starvation salaries?

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that salary level is about the same as that offered to all university graduates in other fields.

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question. Is the Secretary of State saying that this salary is offered to university graduates in other fields? If so, this would call for an explanation, because the Secretary of State knows very well that $4,500 a year is not an adequate salary for a university graduate.

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I may be wrong, but I think that is what is being offered for the beginners.

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. Is the Secretary of State aware that translators for the world fair, with headquarters in Montreal, are getting salaries ranging from $10,000 to $12,000 a year?

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary question to the Secretary of State, because the explanation he gave us a while ago is not quite clear.
With a salary of $4,500 or $4,600 per year, do the beginners get furnished apartments?

maintopic: SALARIES AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF INTERPRETERS AND TRANSLATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will inquire and I will be very glad to inform my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I have made some comments in respect of this very unusual bit of geography, and have suggested that possibly discussions could be held regarding the creation of an international park there, since the principle has been established in the case of Campobello. Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned at six o'clock yesterday, I was explaining our proposal concerning the amendment to the constitution and I was going to deal with the third point, that is, the control over our immigration.
I said then that as the federal government seems to realize more and more the unfairness of its immigration policy and seems willing to improve things in this department which allows criminals to take refuge in Canada, and since Quebec, under the pressure of the opposition, just made a timid first step in that field, it is important to point out that our group, the Ralliement Creditiste, has something to do with this renewal.
Section 95 of the Confederation Act specifically grants to the provinces a concurrent jurisdiction with federal authorities in the field of immigration. Ontario took advantage of this jurisdiction, but Quebec has always ignored it.
Finally, in the fourth point, we ask that the federal government hand back to the provinces the control over taxation. What should one think about it? The federal government always takes the initiative of legislating in various fields, particularly as regards

municipal winter works, which is an encroachment upon the rights granted the provinces by the constitution.
The federal government supervises and controls the acts of the provincial governments in an exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
The federal government is still levying direct taxes, in contradiction with paragraph (2) of section 92 of our constitution; in fact, the opting out formula does not grant the province of Quebec any greater freedom or power in the taxation field.
Our policy is to withdraw from all those joint programs and recover our total freedom in the taxation field.
It is because of such one-sided deals and also because of Quebec's greater needs, since it has to take in hand the destiny of a whole nation and culture; it is because of its priority needs in the field of education and natural resources development; it is because of compensation it has to provide to workers who cannot find employment that Quebec, if it wants to do something about it, is forced today to impose higher taxes than those levied in the other provinces.
It is because of all those policies that Canadians living in Quebec are overtaxed. Quebec has no longer sources of revenue sufficient to look after the needs of the people.
Both federal and provincial pension plans tacitly recognize that the people are overtaxed, since financing of the plan is based upon compulsory savings. But the consequence will be the same because of the higher cost of living it will bring about. In short, we are not upholding the principle of provincial autonomy just because it is a principle but because autonomy, according to me, means that we have reached nationhood.
One may ask why we are taking such a firm stand. Quebec is beginning to feel its feet; it must exercise all the powers granted to the province under the constitution, and if certain measures go against the aspirations of Quebec, it is the right of its citizens to propose an amendment to the constitution.
We do not accept passivity and we are not expecting miracles either, but we want our autonomy to be truly respected, and that is why it is necessary to amend the constitution. We are working toward that goal with much enthusiasm and vigour because we are convinced to succeed eventually.
The question of relations between the two founding races, that is French speaking and English speaking Canadians, is of vital importance but is too often misinterpreted and

misunderstood. It is confused of course with the new currents in economic and social thinking.
A new distribution of powers and a delimitation of taxation fields according to the interpretations given in the confederation pact seem to be needed today.
Let us not be critical of Quebec when it asserts its position in that respect. Other provinces have the right to entertain just as strongly similar views about the jurisdictional and financial structures.
The colonies of British North America agreed to political union in order to eliminate the imperialistic concept. However, our forefathers were not prepared to replace the imperialistic notion by the concept of the American melting pot.
The fathers of confederation wanted the Canadian nation to be based on philosophical principles inspired by Canadian realities.
Canada was to be a country where all political institutions would be designed to protect and favour individuality, to preserve the basis of an association between French-and English speaking Canadians.
The French Canadians value very highly their individuality and their own identity while, according to many people, for the English speaking Canadians, there is a very serious temptation to yield to the lures of their powerful neighbours to the south in the material and cultural spheres.
It is essential for the rest of Canada to realize that today, maybe more than ever before in our history, the French Canadians are determined to survive in North America.
But I am convinced that the very large majority of French Canadians believe in the survival of French Canada within confederation, provided that amendments to the constitution are agreed to.
All Canadians should realize that in helping us, French speaking Canadians, we are preserving our own Canadian identity and thus strengthening the basis of Canada's independence. To be unconcerned about the survival of French Canada amounts to being indifferent about the survival of Canada as a whole.

This is a case that has intrigued the whole of Canada. If this matter goes before the Supreme Court of Canada it may be months or a year or two before it is settled, and the taxpayers will be saddled with the cost of the appeal to that court. I should like to recommend, inasmuch as the House of Commons is the all-powerful authority in Canada, that in the first week of the new session the government introduce a bill granting citizenship to Mr. and Mrs. Bergsma. Mr. Chairman, there are a number of topics that demand immediate explanation from the government, and I only expect to mention a couple on this occasion. There is one upon which I have been seeking a determination and information from the government for some time without any degree of success. I refer to the Atlantic development board and the attitude of that board and this government toward a submission which has now been before the government since March 28, 1964.
Before I go into the details, I should like to preface my remarks with a few comments about this board and about the attitude of this parliament as well as previous parliaments toward the Atlantic area and the special problems that exist in that area. We read in the newspapers today of the fact that while unemployment is not the national problem it once was in this nation, the Atlantic area is still suffering from chronic and high unemployment at a rate that just cannot be accepted in a nation that is dedicated to the welfare of its people. Thirteen per cent of the population of the Atlantic area is unemployed. During the election campaigns of 1962 and 1963, we heard from the Liberals many grand and wonderful stories about what they would do were they elected, to eliminate the problem of chronic unemployment in the Atlantic area. But today we find we are no farther ahead than we were then and this government has now been in office two years less one week.
One of the promises made was to use the Atlantic development board, which the Diefen-baker government conceived and put into effect, in an advantageous manner to eliminate the problems we faced. The first thing the government did after taking office was to indicate to the people of the Atlantic area that the Atlantic development board would no longer be the vehicle by which the problems of the Atlantic area would be attacked and eliminated, but rather that the role would be changed to that of a gap filler with a fund of $100 million available to it, and a life

for an undetermined period after great objection was taken by the official opposition to the proposed date for extinction.
We find ourselves today in the position of having a board that has used up most of the funds that have been made available to it, with no indication as to its future. Indeed, we are finding it most difficult to ascertain from the government what its plans are with regard to the province of Nova Scotia, and with regard to that substantial sum of money that has been allocated to that province for determination by the province as to how those funds might best be used for the betterment of the people. At the same time we find that a grant, if you want to call it that, of $24 million has been allocated to the province of Newfoundland for the development of power at Baie d'Espoir. Only this week we had an announcement from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources concerning what is happening to that power development and what it will mean to the province of Newfoundland. Certainly the members of this house are indeed pleased to see this project going forward at the rate anticipated.
Then, we find that the government of New Brunswick made a submission to the Atlantic development board requesting a grant of $20 million towards the development of power at Mactaquac on the Saint John river. This grant was approved and the project is going forward, although there is still some difference of opinion in the province of New Brunswick as to the merits of this power project. We must all hope, however, it will be for the benefit of the people of that area. In other words, Mr. Chairman, there has been no argument from the government with regard to the proposals made as to how New Brunswick will spend the $20 million or how Newfoundland will spend the $24 million. Indeed, the Atlantic development board and the government both felt that these provinces should and could determine how these sums could best be spent. As a result, we see progress in this field in those two areas.
What is the situation in Nova Scotia? We find, as I stated earlier, that on March 28, 1964 the government of Nova Scotia made a submission to the Atlantic development board as to how it felt the $20 million allocated to that province should be used. Indeed, they made very specific recommendations based on a report prepared by Professor T. Wilson for the Atlantic provinces research board in which he submitted that the $20 million allocated to Nova Scotia could best be used by making

direct grants to industries located in that province.
I should like to read a few of the recommendations contained in the submission by the government of Nova Scotia to the Atlantic development board, regarding industrial incentives. One of the recommendations was to this effect:
Tax incentives which have been made available by the parliament of Canada have not in fact been effective in attracting industry to Nova Scotia. Such tax incentives may affect the choice of location within Nova Scotia by industry which has decided to locate in the province, but the availability of these same incentives in other parts of Canada may actually increase our difficulties in bringing industry to Nova Scotia.
We submit that the most effective incentives are direct subsidies to reduce the capital and settling-in costs of new industries along lines recommended by Professor T. Wilson in a report prepared for the Atlantic provinces research board dated 8 February 1964.
The government of Nova Scotia therefore requests the Atlantic development board to provide the following incentives for manufacturing industry in Nova Scotia: grants up to
(a)	20 per cent of the capital cost of new manufacturing industry;
(b)	33J per cent of the payroll cost of such industry during the first two years of operation.
Such grants will result in substantial expenditures, but these will be a modest part of total government expenditures in this area. Each job created will create additional jobs. The federal government will benefit from resulting increased productivity, increased tax yields and reduced unemployment benefits. Professor Wilson properly emphasizes the importance of incentives being large enough to be effective. We recognize that your board may wish to limit the total amount available for such grants but we emphasize the importance of enough being made available to do the job required in Nova Scotia.
It is important that grants up to the percentages in paragraph 10 be available for new secondary manufacturing industries in such a way that this province could count upon the grants being available without clearing individual cases with the Atlantic development board in advance. It would be of the greatest importance for our provincial officials and agencies to be able to negotiate with industry in confidence and with confidence in the availability of the grants. For this purpose plants for the processing of fruits and vegetables should be classified as secondary manufacturing.
I believe that is a fair indication of what the government of Nova Scotia felt would be the most useful way of using the $20 million allocated to it for the welfare of the people of that area.
On Tuesday of this week I asked the Minister of Transport a question regarding Professor Wilson's report and the recommendations made by the government of Nova Scotia to the Atlantic development board. This was his answer:
Interim Supply
I think the hon. gentleman is aware that the initiative in that matter lies with the government of Nova Scotia; and I am sure they are just as anxious to get ahead with good uses for this money as we are.
If the government of Nova Scotia were to read that reply it would have to arrive at the assumption that it had never made a submission to the Atlantic development board, or that the government, and the minister who is charged with responsibility for answering to parliament for that board are unaware of the submission. Surely there must be some error of judgment in the reply given by the minister, or we must reach the assumption that he is in fact in favour of the government of Nova Scotia making a determination as to how the money allocated could best be spent.
If the latter is the case then I tell the government, approve the recommendations submitted to the Atlantic development board by the government of Nova Scotia, and approve them immediately. The people of Nova Scotia have been waiting for a year for an answer from the federal government, and every day that passes hurts the chances of the government of Nova Scotia to attract industry to the province.
All the time that passes places the governments of Newfoundland and New Brunswick at an advantage over Nova Scotia. I wonder, is it unique that the governments of Newfoundland and New Brunswick, which happen to have Liberal premiers heading them, were able to find a degree of approval, through the Atlantic development board and the federal government, for the proposals they made, while Nova Scotia, which happens to have a Progressive Conservative premier, has encountered delays and less than a forthright answer to its proposal on how the resources of Nova Scotia can best be developed for the people of that area.
The people of Nova Scotia are entitled to an unequivocal yes or no answer. The sooner they receive it the better off will everyone be, and the people of Nova Scotia will be able to decide whether this government is as willing and as interested in promoting their welfare as was the former government. In view of the fact that we do not know when the government will have to give an accounting of itself before the people, it would be well for Nova Scotians to know where they stand with this government.
I should now like to turn to a subject that is quite different and which, in my estimation, has both local and national application. A commission has been established by the

Interim Supply
government to investigate all the implications of broadcasting. The commission has as its chairman, Robert Fowler. That commission will, I understand, report to the government in the latter part of May, according to an answer obtained in the house recently. During the period in which this commission has been sitting, new applications for television facilities available to various areas of this nation have been frozen. During this period we in the Cumberland and Westmorland area of the maritime provinces have been anticipating that we might be provided with alternative television through the facilities of CTV and more specifically through CJCH-TV of Halifax. An application had been made to the board of broadcast governors by CJCH-TV, but unfortunately for the people of our area it was set aside until such time as the Fowler commission brought down its report. So we have been waiting patiently for the report in question in the hope that the freeze would be lifted and that consideration would be given to a new application should one be submitted by CJCH-TV.
During this period some areas of Cumberland county have enjoyed CJCH-TV through a small satellite, weak in many aspects, which has been established just outside the town of Amherst. This satellite has given us a taste of something which has been very palatable and of which we desire a larger portion.
There is another aspect of the matter which is of real interest to me. It is that in my constituency in Nova Scotia, lacking the facilities of CJCH-TV we are in the position of having to depend upon television facilities which are made available through CKCW Moncton and CFCY, in Charlottetown. This has taken the emphasis off my area in Nova Scotia as far as news made available to my constituents is concerned. It is natural that a station based on Moncton and another on Charlottetown should treat Nova Scotia news as secondary. Thus my constituents are not at the present time provided with a news service as satisfactory as that which is available through CJCH-TV. For this reason I am most anxious to see an application by CJCH-TV considered again by the board of broadcast governors. It is my hope that when the Fowler commission reports in May there will be no indication that the temporary freeze on applications now in existence will be continued.
There is one other aspect of the Fowler commission inquiry I should like to men-

tion. It concerns comments, increasingly more prevalent, favouring a ten year charter for the C.B.C. Recently the president of the C.B.C. made a speech in Montreal in which he outlined reasons for which he thought a ten year charter should be made available to the corporation. One of the main reasons, it appeared to me as I listened to parts of his speech, was that the parliament of Canada carried out too many inquiries into the operations of the corporation. Well, this year we are being asked in the estimates tabled for 1965-66 to provide a subsidy or a grant of $99,444,000 of the taxpayers' money to the corporation. This is not an insignificant sum.
Is that inclusive of the loans, or exclusive?

That is exclusive of the loans. The loans are determined on an accounting basis altogether different from loans I would be able to secure. That amount represents an increase in the grant or subsidy of $11,444,000 as compared with 1964-65. I would say it is a substantial increase for a corporation which is now asking us to make a ten year outlay of funds in order that, among other things, the corporation might not have to face parliamentary inquiries. What the president of the C.B.C. is seeking, in my estimation, is a blank cheque for at least a billion dollars and I think that is too much to expect any government to approve especially since there is no guarantee that the government which approved it would be in office during the ten years in which the money would be expended.
Further, there has never been carried out to my knowledge the type of examination of the affairs of the C.B.C. which I would like to see, that is, an examination of the operations of this gigantic colossus from an organizational point of view similar to that carried out by the Glassco commission into government organization. I think that before we are asked to approve an outlay of a billion dollars we and the people of Canada should be given some assurance that the C.B.C. is being operated as efficiently as the taxpayers of this country would like to believe it is. Until we have these answers I do not think consideration should be given to the granting of anything more than we are providing now, and indeed I am becoming very sceptical about the amount we are now allocating to the corporation for its operations.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid
Motions for Papers
before this house a copy of all correspondence exchanged during the past year between the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general or other provincial ministers regarding methods of amending the constitution of Canada; and also for other papers and documents prepared for and presented to the meeting held in October between the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general relating to the amendment of the constitution of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion for the production of papers requests that a humble address be presented asking for all correspondence written during the past year passing between the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) and the provincial ministers regarding the amendment of the constitution to be produced. I do not quite understand what possible objection there could be to this motion. During a previous parliament when another administration was in power I moved a similar motion in respect to papers relating to the constitutional amendment conference of 1960. I have in my hands a copy of sessional paper No. 256 of December 13, 1962 relating to the correspondence concerning the proposals then being discussed, or which had been discussed, regarding the amendment of the Canadian constitution, which correspondence was duly produced.
I realize of course that the production of these documents, so far as they consist of correspondence with provincial governments, can be produced only subject to the consent of those provinces. In actual fact this is precisely what happened when the previous administration was in office, and it surprises and pains me to And that the present administration is more sticky and obstructive in relation to a matter of this sort than was the previous administration. I suggest there is no reason at all for not producing these papers, subject of course to getting the consent of the provincial authorities.
I would point out that the subject matter involved in this motion for the production of papers is one about which the public of Canada is entitled to all facts and information. The public should know where this government stands on the matter, the reasons the government advanced for the adoption of what is now known as the Fulton-Favreau formula, and the views expressed by the different provinces in correspondence in regard thereto.
There is a tremendous and growing concern in Canada about this whole subject of constitutional amendment. History alone requires that this matter should not be dealt with in a hole in the corner manner. I urge

Motions for Papers
upon the government that it make available for historians, for scholars, for constitutional experts and for the public of Canada the correspondence which produced this formula, which has not only been put before this parliament, or will be put before it at some future stage, but which is the concern of every provincial legislature as well. If it be the case that a provincial authority has said something embarrassing or political in this correspondence which I ask to be produced, notwithstanding even that I suggest we are entitled to these papers and documents.
If I were to enlarge on this matter, Mr. Speaker, I would merely be repeating what I have just said. I urge, in view of the transcendent importance of the constitutional amendment formula, and in view of the widespread concern about this matter all across Canada, that this correspondence be not withheld from the people of Canada. I am not asking for new ground to be ploughed or for any deep secrets to be revealed. What I am asking is for no more than that which the last administration were perfectly willing to do. I hope this plea of mine will achieve some response from the government benches, and we will not have to say as a result of any opposition to this motion that the full facts in respect to the amendment formula regarding the constitution are not available to the people of Canada.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, may I say that all hon. members of the house are aware of the keen interest shown by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) regarding the proposed patriation of our constitution, and the amending formula. However, with respect, I think that in making this motion he is confusing the two aspects of the problem. The patriation of the constitution is one problem. The ultimate revision of the constitution or the writing of a new constitution, if such be the trend of events in this nation, is a different problem entirely.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is the same problem.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member is desirous, quite properly, to have as full and as public a discussion as possible of the question of the amendment of the constitution and its patriation; at least, I take that to be so from the wording of his motion. However, I would point out that as an antecedent to any essential and necessary amendment to the constitution there must perforce be discussion with the provinces, irrespective of whether we accept the view that our constitution is in

the nature of a treaty between the various provinces existing at the time of confederation -new partners have, of course, since entered into confederation-or whether we deny, as did Professor Dawson in his work, that this is a type of treaty between the various components of confederation. Nevertheless, in the present circumstances existing in Canada it would surely be intolerable and impossible to effect either the patriation of the constitution or a fundamental revision of the constitution without prior discussion and negotiation, and to large degree agreement with the provinces. Irrespective of how much we may tend toward viewing the fact that the federal constitution and the federal government are supreme, or whether we are of those who believe that this is an agreement by and between the provinces, I think any pragmatic politician would have to say that any sound or pervasive revision of the formula for repatriation would be impossible without prior negotiation and discussion with the provinces.
I noted with interest the views of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) in respect of the measure which was before this house the other day. His very effective and sound argument in this regard was so highly thought out it is quoted editorially in the Ottawa Journal of tonight. As I understood his views, they were that any measures that we adopt with regard to the reallocation of responsibility for sources of revenue between the provincial and federal aspects of our constitution are but a hodgepodge and piecemeal solution to a very fundamental problem in respect of our constitution. He is duly patted on the head editorially tonight for his very sound views in this regard.
That being the case, I think any individual who has the long term well-being of this nation at heart would agree that obviously at this date and at this time there are very fundamental revisions needed in the constitution of this nation. I again return to the pragmatic aspect of how this is to be brought about. I think all hon. members will surely agree that there must first be discussions with the provinces in an attempt to resolve the views of the provinces in the directions in which they would move.
I do not think, in accord with precedents which have been set in this regard in respect of other matters affecting the provinces and the federal government, that this could be done in any public forum. The precedents which determine that negotiations and discussions between provincial governments and

the federal government at the provincial conference table should be held in confidence, unless otherwise agreed to by all parties, are many. How else could there be free and frank discussions, and how else could there be open differences of opinion, where such exist, in an attempt to resolve such differences of opinion, if these opinions and views stated in writing or otherwise were subsequently to be made the subject of public discussion? I suggest with respect that again, if we can analogize to the treaty making powers, surely at this time the dominion-provincial conference in respect of our constitution, again irrespective of our views of the original constitution, is analogous to the treaty making powers. If the treaty making powers were to sit in public and discuss all their documents in public, I think there would seldom be an amicable solution to differences. This is true of both the treaty table and a dominion-provincial conference.
I suggest with respect that the hon. member, who has proposed this motion in good faith because he has had concern about this subject, would be doing a great disservice to the likely ultimate satisfactory resolution of the varying points of view of the provinces and the federal government by insisting on making public all the differences and all the materials which were filed or which were discussed confidentially during the negotiations which have already taken place.
I would point out also, from the standpoint of moral integrity on a question such as this, that the men who came from the provinces to these conferences came clearly on the understanding that the discussions would be held in camera and that there would not be public discussions of their varying views.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. Has he ascertained from anybody in the government, or on his side of the house, whether any attempt has been made to find out if the parties to the conference have any objection to the production of this material? As I have said, I have been made aware of the fact that at a previous conference the attorneys general clearly expressed the opinion that they had no objection to the production of this material.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the very humble and remote place where I sit the government does not inform me as to the views of the provinces on these matters, but I understand that an hon. gentleman on this side of the house, who sits closer to the periphery of power than I, intends to speak 20220-826J
Motions for Papers
on this matter, and that he will be able to resolve the doubts of the hon. gentleman in this regard.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) pointed out, and I think he complained somewhat in this regard, that the papers produced at a prior similar conference were disclosed. I am not sure of the trend of events leading up to that disclosure, but I have had occasion to check the proceedings of those meetings and it may well be that those papers were in fact produced after those conferences had in fact floundered, and when there was no possibility of arriving at a resolution to the problem regarding repatriation of the constitution. Surely that is what happened at the prior meetings- ultimately they broke down. If the disclosure of the papers was made subsequent to the time it was obvious that these conferences had broken down and there could be no solution, then no harm could be done.
I point out with respect to the hon. member that at this time I think all of us have the hope that these discussions will move to the point of resolution. We hope that they will move to the point where, after very close to a century of history, we will soon have a Canadian constitution back in Canada. I do not think any of us want to put any impediments in the way of this very desirable goal.
Speaking personally as a private member I may say that I agree with the hon. member, that at some stage of the proceedings there should be a very full, frank and open discussion before there is any amendment to the constitution, or any fundamental revision made, and before there is a complete rewriting of the constitution to meet the needs and demands of the time.
My personal views are inclined to those of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this regard. I believe there should be a great national conclave prior to the time when we re-write our constitution, or develop our own constitution which I personally hope will be called the Canada Act rather than the British North America Act. While the British North America Act is a great antecedent to a Canada Act, I believe it is time to have a constitution, which is completely and uniquely our own, domiciled here in Canada. I think the events which lead up to the writing of that constitution will be of great moment in respect of the question of national unity. I hope there will by a momentous historical occasion which will lead to the re-writing of the constitution,

Motions for Papers
in which there will be participation on a national level. I hope it will be something more than an agreement between the provincial entities of our confederation, and I hope that the new confederation act will enable direct participation in its amendment procedures by the people of Canada. I am one of those who believe that there cannot be a sound and truly uniting concept of amendment which does not provide for direct participation by the people of Canada themselves by way of referendum, and I hope that such a formula may be implemented in respect of the ultimate resolution of our constitutional problems.
At the time when the constitution is to be completely revised or rewritten I will certainly be among those who agree completely with the concept that the hon. member has envisaged here, that there be full, frank, open, clear discussion in Canada which I hope will be the prelude to a popular discussion by the people of their constitution. I think all of us have remarked from time to time that the American constitution has been to the people of that great country such a bond, such an instrument of allegiance by the people of the United States to their country. I think their flag and their constitution are things to which all Americans pay deference and allegiance and they have been a great bond of unity in that land.
I know that all members of the house hope that our flag, now that we have a uniquely Canadian emblem, will be such a bond to the people of Canada. When we rewrite our constitution and domicile it at home, when we have had these prior, open, public meetings whereby great interest in our constitution can be engendered, I for one hope that subsequent to that time the Canadian constitution will be a linking bond of the Canadian people, a source of pride, a source of unity which will in fact help to keep this nation together in the future. Surely if this concept is to be achieved the type of discussion which the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) envisages will be necessary as a precursor to the fashioning of that new constitution. But I do suggest with the greatest respect that at this time we are but doing the groundwork, the humble spadework, for that great day of the rewriting of our constitution, and this must be done through negotiations between the provinces and the federal government with respect to our constitution as it exists.
There must of necessity be participation by public servants at all levels, and I do not think any of us believe that the honest and
FMr. Greene.1
forthright views of public servants should be brought into public discussion later. I suggest with respect that we will do a disservice to the ultimate resolution of the problem of (a) the patriation of our constitution in Canada and (b) the revision and rewriting of a truly Canadian constitution if we interfere too greatly by insisting on public discussion at this time of matters which are the subject of private negotiations between the provinces and their officials and the federal government and its officials. I suggest that this is the time to be patient, to wait and see the results of these negotiations. Once they are available the resolutions will be made public and I trust that then we will have the kind of public discussion which will lead to a new Canadian constitution domiciled right here in Canada.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that by now the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), who had indicated a desire that the debate interrupted by this debate should continue, will have been convinced of the wisdom of the attitude taken by those on this side, as indicated by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), who thought this hour should not be lost to posterity. In particular, after hearing the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene), whose words in connection with this very important issue are now embedded forever in the transcript of our proceedings, it would seem obvious that our course was the proper and correct one. To put it another way, if this can be regarded as the death rattle of this session of parliament, we want to be able to distinguish in it the words of the hon. member for Renfrew South, the hon. member for Greenwood and others who want to participate in the debate.
I appreciate the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Renfrew South with regard to my modest contribution the other day. I hope he will be impelled to change his mind on this particular issue after I have concluded. I am not going to say very much. While he has expressed one view, I am sure that the notorious flexibility or remarkable elasticity which his party and government have displayed during the course of this session will by no means preclude him from changing his mind after I have completed my remarks.
I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Greenwood that the last government was perfectly prepared to disclose the correspondence in connection with this particular issue

to the extent that it lay within its power to do so. This was a display of the type of statesmanship which one would consider to be appropriate to the last government, and I only hope that the refusal of the present government does not show that the level of statesmanship is not now of the same calibre. I hope we have not descended into political expediency rather than statesmanship in regard to deciding which documents will be publicized and which will not.
The issue before us, Mr. Speaker, concerns not only the government of Canada, not only the governments of the various provinces, but all of the people of Canada. I have no doubt that in those cosy, quiet little discussions held between federal government ministers and officials, and provincial ministers and officials, issues of this kind are considered, and I suppose at times they are considered from the point of view of what is best for the country. I have a shrewd suspicion that while the people of Canada are shown in these meetings in the light that the people who are to participate in the discussions con-siaer them, quite frequently they are considered only as voters and not necesarily as people who have a keen interest in the issue of the constitution and what we are going to do with it. I feel that there should be a great national debate involving all of the people of Canada and I have a desire that as Canadians, whether they are residents of one province or another, they have a vested interest in knowing what takes place at these meetings and what arrangements are made as a result of them.
This brings us down to the particular issue here. It is not an economic issue. This is an issue involving the way in which we are going to divide our constitutional responsibilities and the method by which we are going to amend the constitution without having to encounter the difficulties we have experienced in the past. Under these conditions I feel that the views of the provincial governments should be made known without any suppression as a condition precedent to this debate taking place. After all, we have heard about the constitutional amendment being placed before the legislatures of eight provinces, I think, but there has been a remarkable lack of discussion and a remarkable lack of debate during the course of these proceedings. Only in the province of Quebec, I believe, has there been up to the present time some indication of a very substantial debate.
I think that this is the kind of discussion which should take place at all levels, not only
Motions for Papers
on the national and provincial government levels but at the community level, at service club and chamber of commerce meetings and farm and labour unions. This is a question which is vital and of the essence to all of us, and in my humble opinion it is going to be an issue which will only be decided when there is a unanimity of views reached among a very large majority of the people of Canada, irrespective of whether they live in Quebec, British Columbia, Alberta or Ontario.
In order to have this debate, I think we must have the benefit of the views of all who have been concerned, all who are interested, and all the ministers of provincial governments who have corresponded with the Minister of Justice. For this reason I can see no valid excuse why the government should not be prepared at this time to produce this correspondence.
I am delighted to support the very reasonable suggestion made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), and the reasons which impelled him to move this motion.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext: Can he tell us if, in fact, it would be politically possible to revise the constitution basically without the prior agreement of all the provinces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There appears to be some tendency to enter into a discussion of the merits of the constitutional amendments, and perhaps before making my remarks this afternoon I should make reference to an observation made by Mr. Speaker Michener on March 22, 1962, shortly after the procedure we are following first came into general use. I quote from page 2071 of Hansard for that date:
As I understand it, this motion calls lor the house to order the production of a document described here, the production of which the government resists. The debate is on the issue of whether or not the government is correct in resisting the production of the document. Now, anything that is relevant to that issue would, in my opinion, be relevant to the debate.
Then, Mr. Speaker Michener goes on to point out that there is a very difficult question involved in these motions. On the one hand, it is desirable that the full merits not be gone into, but on the other hand it is desirable that enough of the merits be available so that the house can decide whether or not, in the public interest, the usual procedure followed in the house should be waived. I think it might be useful to remind the house again that it has been the long standing practice in this chamber, followed by the government which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) supported and by the government supported by members on this side of the house, that internal documents of a confidential character should not be made available in response to a motion for the production of papers.
In this respect the parliamentary authorities, going back to some of the most eminent ones, such as Todd, have pointed out the fact that while it is definitely necessary, on the one hand, that the house have all relevant information, on the other hand it is desirable that the procedure not be used in such a way as to make available the essentially internal documents needed for the operation of government, documents produced by the government's own advisers with the intention that they should be confidential. Some of the documents requested by the hon. member in this motion are, without question, documents prepared for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) and others representing the government of Canada from time to time
[Mr. Basford.l
in these discussions, by the officials of the department. They were prepared on a confidential basis. As the hon. member for Greenwood would know from his experience in the law courts, it has been clearly established in administrative law that if documents of this kind, which have been prepared for confidential purposes, are sought for public disclosure, then it is likely the court will refuse their introduction on the ground that the confidentiality or candour which one could expect from the minister's advisers might well be lost. If there were a fear these documents would be made available to the public, that result might follow.
If I may refer again to Todd, we find that if we continue to allow motions to this effect to be passed, the confidential memoranda would merely reappear as memoranda of a personal character, so you would really only arrive at the same result in the long run. Hon. members will recall the cause celebre in this house during the 1958 session when a highly confidential document, in fact one specifically marked "secret", was produced in this house by the government of that day. The seriousness of the matter at that time was indicated to the advisers of the crown, with rather serious consequences, by senior civil servants. I think it must be recognized that unless the government is entitled to take its counsel in private, then the operations of the government generally will be very much prejudiced.
We have an additional factor here, Mr. Speaker, in that the motion seeks not only the production of documents arrived at in confidence for the benefit of the government of Canada but also seeks the production of documents arrived at in confidence for the provincial governments. As the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) pointed out, the feeling of mutual trust would be very much impaired if this parliament were to order the production of documents produced for provincial governments and delivered in discussions which were to be in camera.
Now, the hon. member asks, as one might expect him to ask, why do we not get consent? Who is withholding consent? What provincial governments are refusing? I think it is proper to refuse to answer any kind of cross-examination in that regard because, essentially, all such questions merely hold a gun at the head of provincial governments by suggesting that if they refuse to make these documents public they are trying to hide something which it is not in the public interest to see.

Mr. Brewinr May I ask the hon. member a question? Quite apart from the government of any individual province, is the hon. member able to tell us whether any of the provinces have been asked or have raised any objection to the production of this material?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS ON CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, since you are a member of the bar of Ontario, just as the hon. member for Greenwood is, you will appreciate at once the skill and dexterity with which a craftsman can work. Here he is, trying to start digging out bits and pieces by this masterful type of cross-examination. It was for this reason I carefully pointed out that I did not propose to be drawn into any kind of cross-examination concerning whether or not we were prepared to seek consent, and so on. I think that is an entirely proper procedure on my part.
The hon. member has made a number of statements in public constituting complaints about the procedure followed by the present government in arriving at the formula for amending the constitution, which is now to be found in the white paper recently tabled. Essentially, the basis of the complaint is that the public do not understand the purport of the formula, that the public do not have any idea what kind of arangements were arrived at as a result of the discussions between the attorneys general, which produced the proposed formula. I think any hon. member who has read the white paper on the constitution will realize just how much nonsense is that suggestion. We have, in fact, over a period of nearly 30 years been discussing the appropriate measures to be taken by the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces to render the amending procedure into Canadian hands.
In fact almost the identical wording was first fully debated and made public following the year 1960-61 at the time when the so-called Fulton formula was produced. Prior to the current stage of negotiations, spokesmen on behalf of the government indicated the extent to which the government intended to pursue the development of 30 years in an attempt to achieve an agreement on the basis of the Fulton formula. This, of course, is in fact what happened, and for any person to suggest there has been any particular secrecy, or that there should be public surprise with the end product, is to make a rather bald statement in absolute defiance of the facts on the record.
In fact the hon. member himself had an opportunity to give a very learned address
Motions for Papers
on the subject prior to these particular negotiations, in which he referred at length to his viewpoint, albeit an erroneous one, on the subject of the Fulton formula. Therefore I do not think the question really arises of whether it is in the public interest or not, because of any suggestion of secrecy, that this material should be made public. In fact all the relevant material which, in the interests of good government, can be made public has been on the public record for a long time.
It has been very aptly summarized and put before the house in the form of a white paper, and I do not think there can be any real suggestion that the people of Canada, the members of this parliament and the members of the legislatures, have not been supplied with the necessary and relevant material upon which to arrive at their own conclusions as to the acceptability or not of the constitutional amendment formula.
I think it is worth emphasizing the ultimate, logical conclusion of the proposition which the hon. member put before the chamber. Both here and in other places he has, from time to time, stated that in some way there is an impropriety in the fact that the government has decided to make up its mind on a particular course of action to be followed, and that the government has entered into direct negotiations with the other governments involved in order to arrive at that particular conclusion. May I point out that in this, as in other matters, and in accordance with our parliamentary system, it is our expectation that the government will take the initiative, will first take its own advice and then take the initiative. In making arrangements depending on the nature of the legislation, members of the public, foreign governments or, in this particular case, other Canadian governments which, under our constitution, have an equal sovereignty determined by the provisions of the British North America Act, are taken into consultation. There surely can be no question of the public in any way having their right to comment upon these matters stifled.
In fact the procedure being followed- and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has made reference to this-is that the proposed formula is coming up for public debate in all ten legislatures in the provinces, and in this chamber. In other words, there will be full opportunity for public debate by the elected representatives of the people, full opportunity for public debate in accordance with our system of government,

Motions -for Papers
and the suggestion that in any way this is being pushed down the public's throat, and that the opportunity is not being given to have the issue put relevantly before the public for proper debate, is just nonsense.
I would only suggest that if there is any irrelevance, obscurantism, or any attempt to cast a smokescreen over the important issue involved here, it has been by hon. members like the hon. member for Greenwood, who have been presenting these spurious arguments about the public not being informed.
The hon. member for Peace River made what I thought was a rather extraordinary statement. He said the public were entitled to have some representation in this regard only as voters. I have some difficulty in accepting the implications of that particular proposition. I think if anything has been learned over the long period of English constitutional history to which we have fallen heir it is that the right to act as voters, to cast ballots, is one of the most fundamental rights which any democratic country can have. In fact it is the inability to have that right, it is the fact that a particular group of the community in Alabama has not had that right, that has led to the demonstrations and actions taken by all right thinking persons throughout the United States. For the hon. member to say the public have a right only as voters to pass judgment on this particular formula as though there were something wrong in that is, I suggest, another form of nonsense.
The hon. member for Peace River also said that the views of the provincial governments should be made known. I have already made reference to the fact that the constitutional amendment formula is going to be debated in all of the legislatures, and in each of the legislatures the attitude of the respective provincial government is put, in accordance with our system of government, before the members of the legislature. These views are being made known, and the views of the public generally. The public has had an opportunity over a long period to form their opinions on the proposed amending procedure.
The hon. member for Peace River also said he did not feel any change in this regard should be made until there was a near unanimity of views among the people of Canada. I do not know whether the hon. member for Greenwood shares that opinion. I would be interested to know if he does because, if that is so, he is arguing right into the teeth of the arguments he has previously made. If it had been necessary for a near unanimity of views to bring about confederation in 1867, then

I think it is pretty certain we would still be waiting for it.
There will be great differences of opinion among the people in our country as to what might be the proper procedure to take as an amending formula, just the same as there will be great differences of opinion on many matters. But I suggest the democratic method to which we have given support is that in the long run the government must assume the responsibility of bringing a particular measure to the legislature, seeking the support of the legislature for that measure, and then ultimately assuming responsibility for it before the public. Therefore I suggest that the suggestion of some constitutional convention, some Philadelphia type of gathering, or the suggestion of the St. Jean Baptiste Society for a meeting of the Estates General whereby various groups, lobbies and pressure interests would meet together in solemn conclave, is once again nonsense.
I suggest that the time honoured system we have followed in this country, the system which was followed in 1867 and which led to our confederation, is being followed here, and I submit it is the only sensible system under the circumstances. Hon. members who have read the white paper will have noted the fact that the document which finally became the B.N.A. Act was produced in the same way, by a series of delegates from the various constituent colonies. I suggest the procedure followed, with the document subsequently being submitted for approval to the legislatures of the various provinces, was not only right then but is right now.
Therefore I think it must be clear to all reasonable hon. members that there is no public interest in the government of Canada at this time, pursuant to this motion, making public documents which were prepared in confidence both by the federal government and the provincial governments. I think it is eminently reasonable, and that all reasonable people would agree it is sensible, that the government should not make these available at the present time, and on the basis of these remarks I would hope the hon. member would withdraw his motion.

This is an item relating to subventions under the Cold Storage Act for cold storage warehouses, and the manner in which the subventions have been provided for some years now has made for disagreement. Shortly after the Conservative government took office in 1957 or 1958 they brought into effect a certain restriction with respect to the payment of subsidies under the Cold Storage Act. It was based primarily on the fact that there was, or so it was claimed, a surplus of cold storage space in Canada for agricultural products. It was also based partly

Supply-Agriculture
on the fact that certain so-called free enterprisers saw in the combination of a loan from the industrial development bank and a subvention of one third, I believe, of the total capital cost of the cold storage warehouse, an opportunity to get their hands on large sums of money to build cold storage warehouses with no capital outlay themselves. This was primarily operative in the agricultural products field, and I understand that some of the people who profited greatly from the combination of borrowing and subvention were prominent Liberals. So the Conservative party, looking at all these factors, decided to place some restriction on the amount of the subvention. Subsequently the operation of all subsidies under the Cold Storage Act was suspended during the financial crisis following the 1962 election.
We have contended, particularly since the initial restrictions were imposed following the election of the Conservative government, that one should use different criteria for the operation of the cold storage warehouse subvention in the case of fisheries products from those used in the case of agricultural products. We have contended that they are two distinct food products and that the rules applying to the one should not apply to the other.
When the present Minister of Transport was a mere private member and sat on the opposition side of the house he used to join with me in a plea for special consideration for fisheries products. In fact, it was because of his intimate knowledge of the manner in which cabinets operate that he asked the then Conservative government to make use of the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act to transfer part of the jurisdiction over the operation of the Cold Storage Act from the minister of agriculture to the minister of fisheries so far as fisheries products were concerned. It was our hope that when the Liberals were elected as the government the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would remember the pleas he used to make when he was on this side of the house and, in conjunction with the Minister of Fisheries who is also from the east coast and also used to speak up quite strongly on behalf of the fishermen when he was in opposition, would give the cabinet the benefit of their knowledge and understanding of this matter, with the result that we would get a better deal in the operation of subsidies under the Cold Storage Act. That has not been the case.
I merely wish to pose a question with regard to the reason for this vote of $26,900 and,

second, to make a plea that the government give serious consideration to the matter and take definitive action to split the jurisdiction, thus giving the Minister of Fisheries some authority to determine the granting of subsidies under the Cold Storage Act so far as fisheries products are concerned. In the way the act is administered now, even if there is consultation with the officials of the Department of Fisheries the fact is that the full weight of the concept of the Department of Agriculture as to the way the matter should be handled takes precedence, and this has been to the detriment of fisheries products and fishermen.
I wanted to take a few moments to say again what has been said so often in the house and to indicate that the Minister of Transport was on our side at one time, and that the Minister of Fisheries was also of the view when he was in the opposition that fisheries products were not getting a square deal. I plead with the government to turn their considerate eye upon this problem because it becomes increasingly more difficult as the years go by. I know this is perhaps not the time to ask for a declaration. I also know that even if I asked for one I would not get it. So all I can do is to let my plea fall upon the open ears of the President of the Privy Council and ask him in his responsible position within the cabinet to bring the benefit of his knowledge and experience to bear upon his colleagues, in the hope that better consideration will be given to cold storage warehouses for fisheries products than has been the case in the past. I should also like him to explain the $26,900.

I am sending you this letter as a farmer, and a member of your constituency, in the hope that I may impress upon you the urgent need for something substantial being applied to the government's agricultural policy.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I say that I am talking about subsidies.
The state of economics and prices being received by a vast majority of the farmers has continued declining to a point where they are at a dangerous level, and cannot be tolerated much longer. In this regard I am not relating to farms which never could maintain a good standard of living for a family, for various reasons, but to the average sized farms which have always provided a plentiful food supply for this country; a feature for which the nation can be thankful.
There have always been suggestions, by the experts, that the answer to the farmers' problem is in increased efficiency, which he has done-three

times over in the past few years, more credit, better quality, sales promotion, larger farm units, etc.
Such programs are necessary, always have been and always will be, but they will never function properly until a system is provided whereby a "realistic price" is received by the farmer, for at least the amount that is consumed on the domestic market.
The machinery to make this possible now exists in the farm stabilization act, and if not, then the act should be amended to allow for it. The deficiency payment system provides the means of equitable distribution that farmers receive their fair share of the national income-
A recent survey conducted by M.R.C. Limited, for the C.B.C., clearly indicates that 85 per cent of the urban dwellers believed the farmers should receive more subsidy than they have in the past.

The situation is critical, and we hope that through your representation, and influence to other members, that positive action may be taken.

Although it would seem that the amount of money farmers have been receiving for their overall operations is a great deal more than it was in the past, yet the net revenue has been dropping each and every year for the last two years. I think it is high time, when we are passing money for grants and subsidies, that the government have a close look at what they are expecting of the farmers, the hours of work involved and the contribution they are making to our society as well as to the world. This is an important factor in our economic life. The government should do everything in its power to see that the net income of farmers is increased rather than decreased as it has been in the last few years.
I have said time and time again that the income from certain phases of farming has gone down and down. We who represent agricultural areas in this house know that is true.
