On my own ranch which is of considerable size, embracing 2,800 females and 650 males, 96 per cent of the males have been sterilized.

Regarding the dairy assistance program, the cost to the government this year will be substantial and will amount to something between $65 million and $70 million. This policy has been adopted so that we will not find ourselves in the surplus position we found ourselves in a few years ago. That is a very undesirable situation, as I think everyone will admit. Approximately six years ago we found ourselves with a 17 per cent surplus of dairy products, but in 1964 it appears that the surplus will be only about 2 per cent, or slightly more.
The dairy industry is a very important industry in Canada, and in many other countries, for that matter. We feel that we must have a dairy industry in Canada, but we feel at the same time that the producer must participate and receive fair remuneration. The program announced in the house a day or two ago in respect of dairy farming will not accomplish all those things we think should be accomplished, but will alleviate the situation somewhat. I want to know whether these P.F.A.A. cheques went out by the end of March. Just answer yes or no.

I can only say that as far as I am concerned as Minister of Agriculture the payments have gone out in exactly the same way as they have in previous years. I have not held up any payments. If they have been paid out previously by the 31st of March, that is exactly the way it would have been done.
Are all the payments made now?
I could not tell you.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has referred again tonight to the proposed dairy policy and legislation that will be introduced later. May I once again say that there is concern in some areas over the possibility of this legislation interfering with provincial legislation. This is so in British Columbia. Can the minister assure us tonight that the proposed legislation will not in any way interfere with or supersede provincial legislation with regard to dairy policy?

Mr. Chairman, as has been indicated, the milk situation in British Columbia is quite a bit different in that most, if not

all, of the business is in fluid milk. Therefore this legislation will not affect British Columbia, nor will it affect Saskatchewan to a great extent because we are not changing the fluid milk situation at all.
May I also ask the minister if the stock of butter has been completely cleared out or if there is still a substantial amount on hand at the present time?

The government, of course, buys butter and sells butter and subsidizes the consumer. We buy butter at 64 cents a pound and sell it at 53 cents. Because it is a seasonal operation and in order to take care of the supply situation we have kept five million pounds of butter oil which we thought we should keep and about 75 to 80 million pounds of butter. We could have eliminated the butter surplus completely but it was felt that this would be a safe amount to have on hand. It would appear that we may have a deficit position in so far as butter is concerned in that we will be consuming five or ten million pounds more than we will be producing. This is why we feel that this is a safe amount to keep in store. We felt that we should probably keep about 80 million pounds on hand.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in some difficulty in trying to understand the statement of the Minister of Agriculture. He said that the dairy people in British Columbia are only in the fluid milk business. If that is so, then as a British Columbia member I should like to know why the Fraser valley milk producers association, and others, have sent us detailed letters expressing great concern over the proposed policy and saying that if it is implemented by the federal government it will completely disrupt their operations. In view of the fact that I and others have received letters of this type from the Fraser valley milk producers association, the largest organization in this field in British Columbia, can we have a definite statement from the minister that the federal legislation will not supersede the provincial legislation or that at least there will be co-operation with the provincial authorities in drafting the federal legislation?

I am pleased to assure the hon. member that this will take place. I also received a letter from the president of the Fraser valley milk producers association with regard to a press report he saw. This was before we made any announcement in the house. The situation in British Columbia is
Supply-Agriculture
that it is an importing province so far as cheese and butter are concerned. As a matter of fact, western Canada will import 30 million pounds of cheese from eastern Canada. They are not self-sufficient in cheese. The Fraser valley milk producers are in the fluid milk business. Under the new policy the province will retain its jurisdiction and responsibility. I can assure hon. members that this whole program will be worked out in close consultation with the provinces. I do not think anyone need worry about it. I am in constant touch with the minister of agriculture of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, the point that puzzles me is that the minister keeps reiterating that the Fraser valley milk producers are only in the fluid milk business, whereas those of us from British Columbia at least are well aware that there are other aspects of their business and that a good part of the milk goes into various manfactured milk products. This is the aspect of the matter that is creating some concern, but the minister keeps talking about fluid milk, which to the layman in the dairy field is most puzzling in the light of what we know about the operations of this organization.

Mr. Chairman, British Columbia has always had a pooling arrangement which is operated under provincial jurisdiction. When we supported dairy products last year we did not support any milk surplus to fluid milk, and this program does not support milk surplus to fluid milk. In British Columbia the biggest percentage of the milk is sold as fluid milk, and only that portion which is surplus to fluid milk goes into cream and a small amount of butter and milk powder.
I suppose the dairy industry of British Columbia is in probably the best shape of any in Canada. They have taken the lead a number of years ago, and I assure the hon. member we are in close touch with British Columbia. We are mainly concerned with the supply of fluid milk. If a public utility board says fluid milk costs $5.25 a hundred to produce, we want to see that the producer gets at least 90 per cent or 95 per cent of it. The producer gets $3.50 for milk that goes into manufacturing.
Now, if he is a real good operator, and you have a real good manufacturer, if the producer bargains properly it is possible he will get $3.60 per hundred for milk. If Quebec is going to support milk, as they have indicated they are going to do in their white paper, the Quebec producer will receive around $4 per

Supply-Agriculture
hundred and fluid milk will probably be something like $5.25. I do not believe British Columbia will be unhappy with this program. I am quite sure they will be well pleased with it.
May I ask the minister this question? Can he assure the house that this new policy does not conflict with the B.C. dairy industry act and regulations; that is what they are concerned about.
Yes, I am pleased to assure the hon. member that this will not happen.

The minister has been using a lot of words, but I think he had better consult again with the minister of agriculture for British Columbia. In the first place, the minister said that B.C. milk producers shipped fluid milk. However, there are three pool areas in British Columbia. Outside of these pool areas there are shippers who ship entirely for manufacture. My first question is this: When the dairy producers outside of the three areas ship only for manufacture, are they subject to the same policy the minister announced on Friday?
Second, those producers in the three areas who ship into the fluid milk market have a portion of their milk which goes into manufacture. Is this portion subject to the subsidy policy announced by the minister last Friday?

Well, yes and no, Mr. Chairman. Last year the portion of milk that was surplus to the fluid milk market was not supported, except that portion which found its way into butter. Those producers received the 64 cents. Now, if producers are shipping to the manufacture market, no matter where it may go, they will receive the deficiency payment, that is the difference between the $3.10 and $3.15, to bring it up to $3.30. Then they will receive a lump sum to bring it up to $3.50. If my memory serves me correctly, the proportion of producers who will receive this is something like 2 per cent or 3 per cent of the producers in British Columbia. I may say that about 70 per cent of all these dairy products produced in Canada are now produced in western Quebec and eastern Ontario.
So, the great bulk of the cream producers- we have 75,000 of them in Saskatchewan and 215,000 in Canada-will receive these deficiency payments, and also the lump sum bringing the price of manufactured milk from the $3.10 or $3.15 which is now negotiated with the plants, up to a maximum of $3.50 for those producers who produce from 10,000 pounds to 50,000 pounds.

Again, the minister has used a lot of words but he has not answered my question. In the first place, those producers who are not within the three pools in British Columbia and who ship entirely for manufacturing purposes, are they subject to the subsidies announced by the minister last week?
Yes.

Of those who ship to the pools, their milk is divided into a certain percentage to the fluid milk market and another percentage to what they call class 2 or class 3 milk, which is generally for manufacturing purposes. Does that portion of their milk which goes into manufacture, class 2 or 3, become subject to the subsidy announced by the minister?
Not in British Columbia or in any other province in Canada.
That is an answer.

I have a question with regard to the sale of butter. I understood the minister to say some of this butter was sold at 37 cents a pound, or less. Can the minister tell us if any of this cheap butter was sold in Canada, and if not, why not?

This butter, with the exception of some of the butter oil which was sold several years ago to bakeries, was not sold in Canada. The butter was sold abroad. Had we seen fit to sell it in Canada, we would probably have broken the whole dairy industry. We were supporting butter at 64 cents, and we were selling it at 53 cents. When butter was selling above 60 cents a pound, consumption had dropped to an all time low of 13 pounds per capita. As long as we do not increase the price beyond 60 cents, our consumption will hold up. This year it appears as if Canadians are going to consume 19, almost 20 pounds per capita. We could have put this butter on the market, but I do not believe it would have been good for the dairy industry. The butter was sold abroad. We are still subsidizing the consumer by about 11 cents a pound.
Is butter oil still made available to manufacturers in Canada?

No, there is no butter oil made available now. The only butter oil we have is about five million pounds which we are keeping in case of emergency, just as we keep about four million pounds of powdered milk.

I should like to refer to the operations of the stabilization board, par-

ticularly with regard to eggs and hogs. We know that at the moment the price of hogs looks rather attractive to some people. It is only that way because the price was so low not long ago many of the farmers went out of business. When you take a look at the price of eggs, you think the same thing is going to happen.
I recall that about two years ago I asked the minister if he would bring the various stabilization boards before the agriculture committee at an early date to allow the members of that committee to look into the operations of that act. The program has been under way for seven years now without a chance to look at it. We should have an opportunity to make recommendations to revise the regulations so as to improve this act. I ask the minister if he will give us assurance that the operations of the Agricultural Stabilization Act will be subject to review by a committee during the next session of the house?

I certainly would be pleased to consider this.
In so far as hogs are concerned, I believe they are supported at $23.65, and the Toronto price is running around $27 or $27.65. Now, this is over 100 per cent of the ten year base.
We are supporting eggs at 34 cents a dozen. I agree with the hon. member that it is a most difficult thing to regulate. One must keep the producers well informed because, for instance, in the province of Quebec the production of eggs has increased by something over 25 per cent, and in Manitoba by 17 or 18 per cent. I agree that the sales of chicks are away down, and probably the price of eggs will be a great deal higher, but I would be very pleased to bring the whole act before the stabilization board.

We have heard all about this "considering" business before. Would the minister give a commitment that it will be brought before the committee? For the life of me, I cannot see why he should be reluctant to have members of the house look at the operations of the act. It has been in force for seven years without there being an opportunity to look at it. It was a new piece of legislation and it is not operating sucessfully from the standpoint of producers who have been forced out of the business. Why not say we can take a look at it?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It does seem to me that the point just raised has nothing whatever to do with the item now before us. The item of $57 million now under discussion relates to expenditures for the current year and not the forthcoming year. The hon. member is attempting to deal with the whole program of subsidies on farm products for a forthcoming year, but I suggest that the questions he is raising are far beyond the scope of the item before us.
What amount of surplus butter is in storage, whether in the form of butter or butter oil, and by how much has the stock in storage been reduced during the fiscal year just ended?

If my memory serves me correctly I think we had 239 million pounds in storage. We now have about 75 million pounds of butter and five million pounds of butter oil. This is something less than we estimated we may require, but it is enough for the moment. Our deficit position would likely be between five million and 10 million

Supply-Agriculture
pounds. With our system of buying and selling butter the department feels we should keep between 70 million and 80 million pounds on hand. We have no surplus butter.

1 realize that; so this vote is to recoup the net operating losses of the agricultural stabilization board which, I understand, disposed of something like 140 million pounds of butter in the last fiscal year, and this was paid for from estimates passed in previous years. I do not know the amount realized from these sales, but is it not correct to assume this item would have to be increased by that amount, as if the butter had not been sold and was still carried as an asset?

You will remember that last year we showed the loss on butter and wrote it all off in one big sweep of $120 million. In the last 12 months we sold $36 million worth of butter, which went into the stabilization board revolving fund. This amount of $57 million is the difference between what we buy and sell. I may not be accurate because I am quoting from memory, but I believe the program this year costs $47 million.

I realize that; but my question has not yet been answered. Does the amount realized from the sale of butter that has been in storage remain in the agricultural stabilization fund, or does it go into general revenue?
The amount that is sold?
Yes, the proceeds from what is sold the previous year?
The proceeds of the stored butter went into general revenue.

I want to raise what may be a small point so far as the over-all situation is concerned, but it is an important one to some of the lamb producers on southern Vancouver island and the gulf islands. A $2 subsidy is paid for grade A-l lambs, but it is paid only when a lamb is certified by a licensed abattoir. There is only one such abattoir on lower Vancouver island, and it charges $3.25 for slaughtering, and keeps the hide, which is worth another 25 cents.
The B.C. government has its own meat inspection service, and I wonder if the minister could not make an arrangement whereby lamb producers could slaughter on their farms and take the carcasses to the inspectors of the B.C. government, who could certify them according to the standards set

for grade A-l lamb. I am not asking for an answer; I am only asking the minister to take it into consideration.
I will be glad to do so.

Could the minister put on the record the total amount expected for egg support for the current year, and could he give us a commitment that the operations of the stabilization act will be brought for study before the agriculture committee next session?
I will be pleased to put the amount on the record, and give very careful consideration to the other.
I do not know whether the minister got what I was trying to get across, but so far as I am concerned I do not think there is much use in passing this particular item.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a correction I think he would like to make in Hansard. Referring to the dairy policy which he announced last Friday and referring specifically to the subsidy which is being paid between the $3.50 and the $3.30 the minister stated a few moments ago that this was based on production in 1963-64. I think the minister meant 1964-65 production.
That is right. I shall make it.

I was interested in the minister's assertion that the president of the sugar beet growers has expressed satisfaction with the action of the government. May I ask him whether this is the national president or the Ontario president, or whether both are expressing satisfaction with the subsidized price?
The national president wrote me and the other president telephoned me.

I should like to make sure of this because I know the provincial president in 1962 said the stabilized price of $13.72 was so low as to be an insult to the industry. In view of increased expenses since 1962, is the association now taking the view that an increase of only 63 cents a ton or approximately $8 or $9 an acre is sufficient?

Of course, as the hon. member knows, it is a complicated set-up, now, with the price based on London prices. But a year ago they were receiving up to $17 and $18 a ton for beets. This raises the average. If the producers do a good job of negotiating this could be $15, and it is satisfactory when they figure out just what it really means to them.
May I ask the minister in conclusion whether it is his opinion that the price will be in excess of $15 for the 1965 crop?
I cannot say. It depends on how well the producers negotiate with the factories. I am sure some of our producers are astute enough to see that the price is very close to this amount.

Mr. Chairman, I was most surprised a moment ago to hear the minister draw a bright picture of our farmers' situation. In my opinion, he is not yet aware that in 1964 the basic income of Quebec farmers went down by $4 million.
I submit that before making such inaccurate statements he should take a close look at the situation; that would prevent him from making statements like the one he made recently when he claimed that a Quebec farmer could earn an adequate income with six cows and two pigs. I would say that it is irresponsible statements like that which irritate Quebec farmers the most and make them hate this government.
I was also surprised to hear the minister say that the sugar beet producers were most satisfied with the increase of 63 cents per ton granted them a while ago.
For his information, I must say that the figures I obtained about a week ago is to the effect that there was no contract signed with respect to sugar beet until last week. Producers do not want to sign contracts unless they have a guaranteed price of $16 per ton. In fact, in an article published on February 4, 1965, in Le Courrier of St. Hyacinthe, it is said that to grow an acre of sugar beets, the farmer must spend the sum 20220-827

of $181.85 in administrative and farming costs. They also say that with a minimum price of $16 per ton, the producer could make a net profit of $42.15 per acre.
Mr. Chairman, I should like the Minister of Agriculture to give consideration to the growing of sugar beets and also to a support price for soybeans. As far as the latter is concerned, he could get information and assistance from his colleague from Essex East (Mr. Martin), because, in the past, the Secretary of State for External Affairs devoted particular attention to that kind of product. This is why, today, I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to advise his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, who really needs it.
It is said that two heads are better than one and I think that if the ministers put their heads together, the farmers would benefit.
But I will repeat that up to last week not a single producer had signed a contract with respect to sugar beets, because the producers believe that unless they get a guaranteed price of $16 a ton, it is not worth their while to grow sugar beets.
Although the minister has just depicted a very optimistic picture as regards agricultural conditions, I suggest he is wrong and that he should not keep on misleading the farmers, who merely want to earn a living and secure the share they deserve from the national revenue.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to vote 90d, we are asked to vote an amount of $1,540,000:
90d. To provide for the operating loss of the Farm Credit Corporation for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1965.
Can the minister tell us what those operating losses cover? Are they related to loans which were not paid back? Are they related to an unexpected rise in operating costs or to a difference between the interest rate paid by the Farm Credit Corporation and the one charged to borrowers?

This amount is the operating cost of the corporation. The losses of the corporation due to bad debts is something less than $6,000. The $1,500,000 is the operating cost, and this is the way they handle their bookkeeping.

Is there any explanation for or any particular reason why such a large amount as $1,540,000 is required over and above what has already been provided to cover an operation deficit? I presume that an item had been provided in the main estimates to cover that deficit. Now, a further amount of $1,540,000 is required. Is there any particular reason for this?

Part of this money is in the interest loss, the difference between the 5 per cent and what the government has to pay for money. The other figure is the operating cost, which really is not high when you consider that the corporation now has out something nearing half a billion dollars. The
[The Chairman.]
loans last year amounted to something like $190 million.
Is it safe to say that part of this loss is due to repossession of lands on which there were mortgages?

The enthusiasm is fantastic. We are just completing the first $100,000 loan in the hon. member's province. In Quebec we have some 40 people participating in a loan. I cannot give you the exact number of applications, but the ones being processed are up in the hundreds.
The minister mentioned a loan of $100,000. How many people are involved in that particular loan?
I am not sure the exact amount, but I think something like 20.

I have been very interested in this legislation and I supported it wholeheartedly because it is based on a sound principle. But what has been done in British Columbia to date with respect to this act?
I cannnot tell the hon. member exactly what has been done in British Columbia, but I would be glad to make inquiries and let him know.
The minister mentioned one $100,000 deal in Saskatchewan. Could he tell the committee how many there were altogether, and break them down?
They are just being processed. I cannot do it now but I would be glad to get the information.
I would be glad to give the hon. member this information, including the loans in Vegreville.

The minister has just quoted figures for the province of Quebec. I understand that about 40 persons benefited under the act. Does he mean that 40 persons resorted to this act? We know that three persons can form a syndicate. Does he mean that ten syndicates or 40 persons obtained loans in the province of Quebec?
The hon. member misunderstood me. When I said there was one loan being processed in Quebec, 40 farmers were involved in one syndicate. Three farmers is the minimum syndicate.
Item agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to give the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works an opportunity to show his mettle. On March 311 addressed a question to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works in order that I might reply to many questions which have been directed to me by people in my constituency who are concerned about the particular and unusual situation. My question was:
Will the parliamentary secretary inform the house as to whether his department accepts responsibility for replacing wharves, launching ramps, rip-rap. pilings and dredging on the completion of the Columbia river treaty projects?
Naturally the people of my district are very concerned about the effect that the Columbia river treaty will have on their lives and their communities. They are also concerned about the clearing of the basins behind the High Arrow, Mica Creek and Duncan lake dams according to the standards established by the west Kootenay rod and gun association, which standards were later endorsed by the British Columbia fish and game federation.
However, the people who still reside in what is left of various communities between Robson and Revelstoke are anxious to know who is responsible for rebuilding the various wharves, launching ramps and other facilities which to date have been undertaken at the expense of the federal Department of Public Works. As far as one can judge at the present time, wharves or launching ramps will be required at Deer Park, Broadwater, Edgewood, Needles, Fauquier, Burton, East and West Arrow Park, Nakusp, St. Leon Hotsprings, Halcyon Hotsprings, Galena Bay, Shelter Bay and Revelstoke.
In addition, the federal Department of Public Works has expended over a period of 60 years thousands of dollars on rip-rap to prevent the erosion of the shores of the lakes or the river at two or three points. The department has installed piling for the convenience of tugs and other watercraft. The Department of Public Works has also undertaken the dredging of any channels necessary between the upper and lower lakes for the safe passage of tugs and other watercraft during low water.
It is because of my constituents' concern that I was asked to ask the minister for a statement of policy in connection with the Columbia river treaty related to the re-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion building of the wharves, docks and other facilities that will be required. The residents are working at the present time for a paved highway from Revelstoke to Robson in order to connect the trans-Canada highway with the southern provincial highway and to serve those small communities that, in some instances, will be left after the flooding has taken place.
I keep in touch with some 250 people in my district on this question. Some of them write me every day about the problems that concern them, whether it be compensation, river basin clearing or something else. They keep me informed about their problems. They say they are getting the runaround from the B.C. hydro and power authority. They deplore the lack of information and they certainly deplore the lack of planning on the part of the provincial government before the treaty was signed. They are simply groping forward blindly, as it were.
My question is this: They want to know to whom they should appeal for the rebuilding of these wharves and other facilities which will be necessary before the Columbia river project is completed. If it is to the federal authorities, they know with whom to deal. If the responsibility is that of the B.C. hydro power authority, then they will soon get into action to present their case to that authority.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) stated, he raised this question yesterday. I am not going to repeat the question because he has put it on the record again. When he finished asking the question, the Speaker interjected and stated this was a proper question for the order paper. The hon. member for Kootenay West intervened and said, "that was really a dud". I do not know what he meant by that. Perhaps he was classifying the subject matter of the question, although I believe he said he had no reference to the subject matter- at least I hope not.
I realize the hon. member has had many representations from people in his constituency who are worried over what will take place in relation to this Columbia project. I cannot tell him at the moment whose responsibility it is to see that these installations are replaced or that new ones which may be required are built. I shall make inquiries and let the hon. member know as soon as I get the information so that the people in his constituency, and the hon. member himself, will be able to direct their efforts into the proper
